Documentation.UserDocu: This is the Material class

Set(string) -- Set the material.
The material must be one of the following values: Brass, Bronze, Copper, Gold, Pewter, Plaster, Plastic, Silver, Steel, Stone, Shiny plastic, Satin, Metalized, Neon GNC, Chrome, Aluminium, Obsidian, Neon PHC, Jade, Ruby or Emerald.
Ambient color
Diffuse color
Emissive color
Specular color
Shininess
Transparency

Whether the values carry the PBR reading rather than the Phong one: DiffuseColor is the base colour, Shininess the roughness, SpecularColor the F0 tint with the metallic factor in its alpha.
Setting it CONVERTS the values, so the surface keeps looking like itself in the other model; only the specular colour, which Phong alone can state, is lost on the way back. Materials read from a ShapeAppearance list carry the list's mode, and assigning materials to one gives it the mode of the first -- the list holds a single mode, so any further entry is converted to it.
The metallic factor, riding the specular alpha. Reads 0 on a Phong material, which has no metals; writing one converts the material to PBR first, since stating a metallic factor decides the mode.
The roughness. On a Phong material it reads as the Blinn-Phong derivation of the shininess; writing one converts the material to PBR first, as Metallic does.

The surface finish pattern by name: "" (none), "knurl", "knurl-straight", "brushed", "blasted" or "turned". An unrecognised name reads back as "".
A finish states what was done to the surface, not how it shades, so it survives every conversion between the Phong and PBR readings. Size it with FinishPitch, FinishDepth and FinishAngle; setting the pattern to "" clears all three.
Surface finish feature spacing, in millimetres.
Surface finish peak to valley depth, in millimetres.
Surface finish lay direction in degrees, within the pattern frame. A lay has an axis rather than a direction, so the value wraps into [0, 180).

The texture maps as a dict of slot name to content hash. The slots are "basecolor", "metallic-roughness", "normal", "emissive" and "occlusion", and a slot the material does not state is absent rather than empty; assigning a dict replaces every slot, so an absent key clears one.
A dict rather than the five scalar attributes the finish uses: the slots are five of one thing, where a finish is four different ones.
The values are CONTENT HASHES, not paths. The bytes live in the document's file store, which is what lets two slots -- or two objects -- name one image and cost one file; a slot names content the store already holds.
Which image is pasted on a surface is not a reading of the shading slots, so a texture survives every conversion between Phong and PBR, as a finish does. Position it with TextureScale, TextureOffset and TextureRotation.
Texture coordinate scale, as (u, v). glTF states this per material, in KHR_texture_transform, and it applies to every map at once.
Texture coordinate offset, as (u, v).
Texture coordinate rotation in degrees. A texture rotation is a direction rather than an axis, so the value wraps into [0, 360) -- unlike FinishAngle, which wraps into half of that.

The embedded texture image of the material, as the string upstream FreeCAD stores it in (the encoded bytes of an image file, base64 in every material card that has ever held one).
The render engine PAINTS it: a per-face appearance whose entries name different images puts each one on its own face, laid out in that face's projection frame at ViewObject.Render_FaceTextureScale millimetres per tile. Coin's own GL path draws none of it -- it binds one texture per draw and has nowhere to put a palette.
The path of the material's texture image, read and painted exactly like Image -- which wins if both are set.
The identity of the material card this material came from. Carried, not used, exactly like Image -- and it is what makes two appearances the same appearance whatever their colours currently say.

The MaterialX document set this look is shaded by, as the content hash of its manifest -- or an empty string when the look is the colour slots alone. The manifest names the document and its image maps by content; the bytes live in the document's blob store, held by the property that stores this appearance.
